title: Why the 1990s stalled: data, compute, vanishing gradients
story:
Three things were missing and only one of them was interesting.

Data and compute are the boring two. There were no labelled datasets of the size these methods need, and no hardware cheap enough to train on them if there had been. Those are constraints that time removes, and time removed them.

The third was a specific defect with a cause, and it was diagnosed rather than merely complained about. Sepp Hochreiter's 1991 diploma thesis at the Technische Universitaet Muenchen formally identified the reason for the training failure, now called the vanishing gradient problem, which affects many-layered feedforward networks and recurrent networks alike. With standard activation functions, cumulative backpropagated error signals either shrink rapidly or grow out of bounds, decaying exponentially in the number of layers. His supervisor later described the thesis as one of the most important documents in the history of machine learning.

The mechanism is short enough to hold. Training computes each parameter's gradient by multiplying local derivatives along the path from the loss back to that parameter. Multiplying many numbers each smaller than one gives something very small, very quickly. So a parameter twenty layers from the loss receives a signal that has been attenuated twenty times over — not slightly, but by a factor that falls off exponentially in the depth. The early layers receive almost nothing and therefore learn almost nothing, while the late layers train normally. The network appears to be training. A number goes down. Most of the network is inert.

Note that the same argument in the other direction gives the opposite failure: if the local terms are larger than one, the product explodes and the updates are enormous and useless. The instability is symmetric, and depth is what amplifies whichever side you land on.

The recurrent case is the same problem wearing different clothes, and it is worse. A recurrent network applied over a sequence is effectively deep in the length of the sequence, so a dependency spanning many steps has a very long path, and the attenuation applies along all of it.

Bengio, Simard and Frasconi made that precise in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks in March 1994, showing why gradient-based learning faces an increasingly difficult problem as the duration of the dependency increases — and exposing a trade-off between efficient learning by gradient descent and latching information for long periods. Approached as a question about dynamical systems, their result is that either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish.

That last sentence is the one worth keeping, because it is a much stronger claim than the usual telling. It is not that long dependencies are hard to learn in practice and might yield to better optimisation. It is that the property needed to hold information stably across time and the property needed for gradients to survive the journey are in tension with each other. You can have one or the other.

Which reframes what the decade's failure actually was. The field had a method whose difficulty had been characterised precisely, with a proof that the obvious fixes could not work, and the response was largely to conclude the approach was a dead end. The characterisation was correct and the conclusion drawn from it was not, because a trade-off between two properties invites an architecture that separates them — which is what eventually happened, rather than better optimisation of the same design.

So the honest reading of the stall is that two of the three obstacles were waiting on the world to change, and the third had already been given the analysis that would eventually solve it, several years before anyone acted on it.

problem.name: Signal attenuated by depth
problem.shape: A parameter far from the loss must receive a usable training signal through a long chain of multiplications.
tell: a deep network trains no better than a shallow one
the loss falls while early layers barely change
a recurrent model handles short dependencies and not long ones
training diverges with large updates rather than converging
problem.move: Treat it as a property of the path length rather than a tuning problem: the gradient is a product of local terms, so it shrinks or grows exponentially in depth. Look for architectural remedies that shorten or bypass the path, because better optimisation of the same design cannot remove an exponential.
problem.invariant: A gradient is a product of local derivatives along the path from the loss to the parameter, so terms below one shrink it exponentially in the path length and terms above one explode it. Depth amplifies whichever side you land on.
problem.breaks: For recurrent models the result is stronger than a practical difficulty. The property needed to hold information stably across time and the property needed for gradients to survive the journey are in tension — either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish — so this is a trade-off to be designed around rather than an obstacle to be optimised through.

cost.time: diagnosing it requires inspecting gradients by layer, since the loss falling says nothing about whether early layers are learning
cost.beats: training deeper and hoping, which is cheap and leaves most of the network inert, and staying shallow, which trains reliably and gives up what depth provides

problem.practice: Take a deep network and record the average magnitude of the gradient at each layer during one training step. If it falls off sharply toward the input, the loss going down is telling you about the last few layers and nothing else.

beats.broke: Deep and recurrent networks could be written down and could not be trained, and the failure was read as evidence the approach was wrong rather than as a defect with a cause.
beats.fix: Identify the cause precisely — the gradient is a product of terms along a path, so it shrinks or grows exponentially in that path's length — which makes the remedy architectural rather than a matter of optimisation.
beats.cost: For recurrent models it is a trade-off rather than an obstacle: either the dynamics are not robust to noise, or the gradients vanish, so one of the two properties must be given up by design.

interview.q: Why does the training signal fail to reach the early layers of a deep network, and why is the recurrent case worse?
interview.trap: Treating it as slow learning that more training fixes. The attenuation is exponential in depth, so the early layers are not learning slowly — they are receiving almost nothing while the loss falls on the strength of the late layers.
